title: Living at Home During a Remodel: A Household Plan
description: Plan meals, bathroom access, pets, work hours, storage, and contractor communication before living through a home remodeling project.
imageAlt: Small backyard deck with black railings beside sliding glass doors

sections.heading: Decide what the house must provide each day
paragraphs: Living at home during a remodel is a planning decision, not simply a way to avoid moving. The question is whether the parts of the house available to you can support ordinary life while construction proceeds. A room that looks separate on a floor plan may still share an access route, utilities, or noise with the work area.

Start with a household conversation before demolition is scheduled. List where everyone will sleep, eat, wash, work, and enter the house. Then review that plan with the contractor for each construction phase. Some projects may require time away. Agree on how that decision will be made rather than assuming the arrangement will remain workable from beginning to end.

sections.heading: Map household routes and construction access
paragraphs: Sketch the rooms being remodeled and the spaces you expect to use. Mark the doors, hallways, stairs, and outdoor routes connecting them. Ask where workers will enter, where deliveries will land, and which areas will be unavailable. Check whether the path to your laundry, garage, or only bathroom crosses the proposed work area.

Discuss how the separation between household space and construction will be maintained and who communicates changes. Do not treat a barrier as permission to stay during every activity. Ask the contractor to explain when access will be restricted and when the area can be used again. Children and visitors should have a simple, consistent rule about staying out of the work zone.

sections.heading: Make a realistic plan for meals and washing
paragraphs: For a kitchen project, write out a typical day's meals using the space that will remain available. Think about refrigerated food, drinking water, dishes, and rubbish, not just cooking. Choose a practical household area away from construction, and review any temporary appliance arrangement with the project team before relying on it. Avoid planning meals around equipment that will be disconnected.

For a bathroom project, identify which fixtures will remain usable and how everyone will share them. If there is no suitable alternative bathroom, discuss arrangements away from home. Ask for notice of expected utility interruptions and a contact if an interruption lasts longer than anticipated. Keep essential toiletries and medications accessible outside the work area.

sections.heading: Treat dust and sensitive household needs as planning topics
paragraphs: Ask about dust containment, cleanup responsibilities, and restrictions during work before agreeing to an occupancy plan. Tell the contractor about household circumstances that could affect whether staying home is practical. If a household member has a health condition, seek advice from their healthcare professional about the proposed arrangements instead of assuming a closed door resolves the concern.

For pre-1978 homes, EPA recommends hiring a contractor certified and trained in lead-safe work practices for renovation work. Its consumer guidance explains that disturbing lead-based paint can create hazardous dust. Share the home's age and ask how applicable lead requirements and occupant protection will be addressed. Do not remove containment or clean construction debris yourself without the responsible professional's direction.

sections.heading: Give pets, work, and deliveries their own arrangements
paragraphs: Pets need a location that remains secure when exterior doors open repeatedly. Decide who moves them before workers arrive, where they can go outside, and what happens if their normal route is blocked. If the work makes that arrangement unreliable, consider care away from the property for the affected days.

For working from home, explain which meetings require quiet and ask what noisy activities are expected. Keep another work location available when necessary; a crew cannot always move a task around a call. Redirect deliveries away from material storage, and agree on parking so household vehicles do not block access needed for the day's work.

sections.heading: Use a short weekly household check-in
paragraphs: Ask for a regular update covering upcoming access changes, deliveries, utility interruptions, and decisions needed from you. Keep these household notes alongside the construction schedule. Confirm the best person to contact and how urgent issues should be raised. A brief, predictable exchange is easier to manage than rediscovering the same questions every morning.

At the end of each phase, reassess whether the arrangement still works. Allow room in your personal plans for meals elsewhere, storage, or temporary accommodation if needed. Bring these practical requirements to your estimate with Tubro Construction. They help define a project conversation that includes the people living in the house as well as the rooms being changed.
